summary: Squirrel Point Light: a shingled 1898 river light at a sharp bend of the Kennebec, built with a keeper's house; automated around 1981, now held by a citizens' group.

lens.where: Given to the Museum at Portland Head Light (Citizens' history)

structures.note: Octagonal wooden frame tower, shingled; gallery 1899; bell house 1902. USLHS gives 25 ft from base to lantern centre.

access.note: USLHS record: not open to the public. Citizens for Squirrel Point holds a Coast Guard license to provide access for educational purposes (Citizens' history). Check with the group before going.

facts.agency: Citizens for Squirrel Point (owner per USLHS; the Citizens' history describes a 2005 court ruling and a Coast Guard license); the Coast Guard maintains the light as an active aid to navigation

events.note: Light-House Board proposes a fixed red light with a white sector at Squirrel Point, estimated at $4,650
Act of 2 March 1895 appropriates $17,000 for the Kennebec River lights, including Squirrel Point

Title to the land acquired; contract let; completion expected by February 1898
Octagonal wooden tower, two-story keeper's house and barn built
Station put into service in 1898 (NRHP); LighthouseFriends quotes the 1898 report on a lens-lantern
Gallery with railing built around the lantern; boat slip and plank walks
Boathouse and boat slip built with the $1,620 appropriated in 1900; barn and fuel house moved
Fifth-order Fresnel lens installed (Citizens' history; USLHS gives 1902 as original lens year)
Gable-roofed bell house built on the tower
Citizens' history says 'fully automated in 1979'; sources disagree
USLHS gives automation in 1981; last keeper left in 1981 (LighthouseFriends)

Mike Trenholm first sees the station and forms Squirrel Point Light Associates (LighthouseFriends)

Federal court rules for Citizens for Squirrel Point in its reversion suit (per the Citizens' history)
Power converted from electric to solar; fog horn disconnected (per the Citizens' history)

corrections.why: USLHS gives 33 ft as the height of the light above mean high water (about 10.1 m). LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane 25 ft above the river (7.6 m). Sources differ; the record uses the river figure. A human should decide which the record should hold.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1979 (Citizens' history), 1981 (USLHS record, and the last keeper's departure in 1981 per LighthouseFriends), 1982 (NRHP nomination text, OCR). Not resolved; the story gives all three.

USLHS lists Citizens for Squirrel Point as owner. LighthouseFriends names Squirrel Point Light Associates (1996 Act of Congress, 1998 deed). The Citizens' history names Squirrel Point Associates (1996) and a 2005 court ruling in its favor. Chain of title not resolved.

notes_for_editor: (0) No woman keeper, or family member who kept the light in her own right, appears in the USLHS roster or in the sources read for this station. (1) Automation date conflict: 1979 (Citizens), 1981 (USLHS and LighthouseFriends' keeper timeline), 1982 (NRHP OCR). (2) Ownership and deed history conflict across the USLHS record, LighthouseFriends and the Citizens' history; the story reports each and says the chain of title is not settled. (3) The Citizens' history says President Cleveland appropriated $4,650 in 1895. The Light-House Board's 1895 report shows $17,000 for the Kennebec group; $4,650 was the Board's 1892 estimate for the Squirrel Point light. The story uses the Board's figures. (4) Focal height: 25 ft above the river (LighthouseFriends, record 7.6 m) against 33 ft above mean high water (USLHS). See corrections. (5) The 1898 and 1902 Light-House Board annual reports are not in the local corpus. The 1898 'lens-lantern' description and the 1902 lens change are cited to LighthouseFriends, which quotes those reports; they are secondhand here. (6) The Kennebec Journal of 18 December 1897 says 'The lighthouses are 19 feet high from lantern to base.' It does not give a figure for Squirrel Point alone, so the figure is not used. (7) No storm, wreck or rescue tied to this light turned up in the sources read, so the story has no storm chapter. (8) Keepers after about 1960 (Skolfield, Robicheau, Reynolds, Reed, Maddox, Burns, Samuelson) appear only as the roster prints them or with their public role; LighthouseFriends' family anecdotes (the deer story, the children, Annette Skolfield's letter) are left out. Mike Trenholm is named as founder of the group only. (9) Roster line 'Mark Samuelson (1971-at least 1972)' is flagged to_approx. (10) The NRHP OCR reads 'It station was automated in 1982' and is quoted as 'was automated in 1982'. The OCR of the 1898 construction paragraph is clean. (11) The record's 'Iso W 6s' characteristic and range (9.0 nm) were not verified in any source read for this story, so facts omit the characteristic. The Citizens' 'alternating three seconds of light and darkness' is quoted in the story as their description. Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: (a) The 1892 report's lens-lantern sentence is read from a scan where the OCR gives 'fixexi' for 'fixed'; the story quotes 'fixed', as printed. (b) Suit date: the Citizens' history says 2002; LighthouseFriends says the group was formed and sued in 2003 (April). The story gives both. (c) Owner: USLHS lists Citizens for Squirrel Point; LighthouseFriends lists the Coast Guard. The story gives both. (d) The 1892 report footnote now cites the scan pages (377-378) that the corpus confirms, not printed page numbers, which the OCR could not confirm. (e) The 1901 appropriation was applied 'in part' to the boathouse; the story now says so. (f) The Citizens' 'treaty conference' wording is theirs; LighthouseFriends says only that Shute 'held a conference'. (g) The Cleveland $4,650 appropriation in the Citizens' history is not used.
